newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain truck strike gravely damages economy - cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Spain truck strike gravely damages economy - cabinet.

text.p: Spain's government said on Friday a nine-day-old truckers' strike was inflicting "grave damage" on the economy.
Development Minister Rafael Arias Salgado, speaking to reporters after the weekly cabinet meeting, pledged the government would guarantee unimpeded travel on its roads.
"This is a savage and unjustified strike which is causing grave damage to the national economy," Salgado said.
"I want to say the government will guarantee unimpeded travel on on Spanish roads," he added.

Salgado said the strike was led by a "violent and radical minority". Earlier, the minister had intimated the strike was being manipulated from behind the scenes for reasons unrelated to the strikers' demands.

Fedatrans, the union which initiated the strike, issued a statement on Thursday denying it was linked to Herri Batasuna (HB), the political arm of the violent Basque separatist group ETA which has been blamed for a wave of deadly attacks recently.
The strike to demand better labour conditions and lower fuel prices began in northern Spain, home of the autonomous Basque country. Other regions were also involved from the start.
The action was burgeoning into a full-blown economic crisis by Friday.
The agriculture sector has lost some 20 billion pesetas ($140.3 million) so far with milk, meat and vegetables worst hit, the farmer's cooperative CCAE estimated on Friday.
The Economy Ministry warned a continuation of the strike would cause a steep increase in fish and produce prices.
The strike looked set to broaden with taxi unions calling on members to join the strike on Monday.
Strikers have choked roads in the north, cut off supplies to many areas and forced factories to shut.
By Friday, the chaos was spreading south.
In a reprise of the French truckers' strike last year which disrupted much of Western Europe with a 12-day blockade, Spanish drivers are demanding a revamp of the sector.
They want the retirement age lowered to 60 years from 65 and are pushing for curbs on surging fuel prices, a revision of tariffs and recognition of professional illnesses.

The cabinet introduced on Friday deregulatory measures aimed at lowering the cost of fuel distribution, a step which leading union Fedatrans welcomed. But the union made clear it would not call off the strike after the decision.

"The measure is one we requested but we're also asking for other things and aside from that we'd like to have professional fuel prices, with a subsidy, such as other sectors like farming and fisheries," said Fedatrans spokesman Jose Manuel Martinez.
Service stations had warned before the cabinet decision they too would take action if diesel prices were lowered.
"This would mean the total ruin of 80 percent of service stations," said the Spanish Confederation of Service Stations.

The government criticised Fedatrans for boycotting negotiations to end the strike. Representatives from the development, labour, economy and industry ministries met a number of transport associations on Thursday but Fedatrans refused to go.

"An end to the strike will only be achieved if the cabinet calls an urgent meeting to create an interministerial commission with powers to coordinate restructuring of the sector," Fedatrans said in a statement.
Meanwhile, truckers tightened their grip on Spain's roads on Friday and blocked ports as the strike spread.
Thousands of trucks lined the hard shoulders of main roads and pickets initimidated any drivers who dared to pass.
With truckers blockading border crossings, hundreds of foreign drivers also found themselves caught up in the jam.
More than a thousand Portuguese trucks were stranded at the border at Vilar Formoso and Caia, and hundreds of French trucks were also stuck at Behovia-Irun, local media said.
